entries.narration: Apache Spark is an engine for processing data that is too big, or too slow to process, on one machine. You describe what you want, in DataFrame code or in SQL, and Spark works out how to do it. Its optimizer, Catalyst, rewrites your query into a faster plan. The driver splits that plan into tasks, one per slice of the data, and executors run the tasks in parallel, on the cores of one laptop or on hundreds of machines, keeping data in memory where it can and spilling to disk where it cannot. The same engine sits under four interfaces. DataFrames and SQL for batch work, which is most of this course. Structured Streaming, which runs the same DataFrame code on data that keeps arriving. MLlib, for models trained on all of the data. And you can write it all in Python, SQL, Scala, Java or R; this course uses Python, PySpark. Spark does not store anything itself: it reads and writes files and tables in Parquet, CSV, JSON, Delta, Kafka topics and databases. It runs on your laptop, on a cluster of its own, on Kubernetes, or as a managed service like Databricks, Amazon EMR or Google Dataproc. The code does not change between them, which is why we can learn it all on one machine.

We will learn Spark by building one thing: the data platform of Shopwave, a fictional online store. Its data comes from four systems. The shop's database holds orders, customers and products. A payment provider sends a Parquet file every day. A tracker on the website records every click, first as JSON files and later as a live Kafka stream. And the warehouse sends returns as a CSV file in an old encoding. All of it comes from a seeded generator, so every run of every step in this course produces exactly the same data, and every number on screen is one a real run printed. The data is not clean, on purpose: there is a Black Friday twenty times bigger than a normal day, one product that is fifteen percent of all sales, a schema change in June, duplicate and late events, a bot, unpaid orders and malformed rows. Each one is a lesson waiting to happen. The platform grows in layers. Bronze lands every source as it came. Silver cleans and conforms it. Gold is a star schema the business can ask questions of. On top of it we build analytics, live revenue and abandoned carts from Kafka, and product recommendations. Then we measure it all at full scale, and ship it: tests, quality checks, and a real cluster.

If you know Python, you know pandas, so why learn Spark at all? This lab answers with a measurement. It computes revenue by country from Shopwave's order exports at scale factor one, first for one day, then for the whole year, in pandas. One day is a few thousand lines and a few megabytes: instant. The whole year is over three million lines, and pandas holds every one of them in memory at once, several times the size of the files on disk, because that is how pandas works: a DataFrame is in memory, in one process. That is fine today. But ten years of history, or ten shops, needs ten times the memory, and at some point no single machine has it. Then Spark runs the same report. Its data is never all in memory at once: it streams through four tasks, each holding only its own slice, so memory is set by the size of a task, not the size of the data. Ten times the data means more tasks, or more machines, and the same code. Spark has a cost: a JVM to start and a plan to make, which is why on one day of data pandas wins easily. The rest of this course is about when that cost is worth paying, and how to make Spark fast once it is.

Shopwave is an online store, and its data team has a problem: a year of orders, clicks and payments, and questions nobody can answer quickly. We will build the platform that answers them, with Apache Spark, starting from an empty project. The editor shows what we start with: one file per day of orders, exported every night from the shop's database. Each line is one order: its id, when it was placed, the customer, their country, its status, and the total in euros. October holds thirty one of these files. Spark is a program for the Java virtual machine, so the first question in the terminal is which Java we have: version twenty one, which this version of Spark supports. Then the same start as any Python project: a virtual environment, activated, and one requirement installed, pyspark, pinned to version four point two. Look at the side pane to see what that one install brought. The pyspark package is the Python API we will write against. Py four J is a bridge: every Spark call we make in Python is carried across it to the Java side. And the jars folder holds two hundred and seventy seven jar files. That is Spark itself, written in Scala, and the reason this one package weighs four hundred and eighty five megabytes. So pip install pyspark does not install a client for some Spark somewhere: it installs all of Spark, ready to run on this machine. The one thing it cannot bring is Java, which runs those jars. With Java, PySpark and a month of orders, we can run the first job.

Every Spark program begins by building a SparkSession, and this is ours. Master local four says: run Spark on this machine, with up to four tasks at a time. The app name labels the run. The last setting points Spark at a small log configuration we added in the conf folder. Spark logs a great deal about its own work, and that file sends all of it to a log file, so the terminal shows only what our job prints. Get or create starts Spark: the Java side launches behind the scenes, and the session is our way in. Then one line reads the first of October's orders. Header true tells Spark that the first line holds the column names. What comes back is a DataFrame: rows with named columns, much like a table. Show three prints the first three rows, as a small grid, and the terminal confirms it is only showing the top three. The first line of output is not ours: it is a notice from the Java virtual machine, which appears every time Spark starts, and is harmless. Then the last line prints the column types, and the side pane lays them out. Every column is a string. The order id, the timestamp, even the total. A CSV file is only text, and Spark does not guess types unless we ask it to. Strings are fine for printing, but we cannot add up a string, and that will matter in a moment. Course three gives the orders a real schema. For now, we have Spark running, and a month of data it can read.

Before we go further, where does a Spark job actually run? This lab counts October's paid orders, then asks Spark what it did, and every number in this picture is its real answer. Start on the left. Our program is a Python process. Each Spark call crosses py four j into the Java side, where the driver lives. The driver does not process data itself. It turns our code into a plan, and when we ask for an answer, it splits the work into jobs, the jobs into stages, and the stages into tasks: one task for each partition of the data. The tasks run on executors. With master local four, there is one executor, inside the same Java process as the driver, with four task slots, so four tasks run at the same time. On a cluster, executors run on other machines, and the code does not change at all. On the right is the data: thirty one small files, which Spark packed into four partitions, one for each slot. Now the lab's output, at the bottom. Count found one thousand three hundred and eighty six paid orders, and the table shows the work behind it. Job zero is the read: one task opened one file to learn the column names from its header. Then count ran as two stages. In the first, four tasks ran side by side, each counting the paid orders in its own partition. In the second, a single task added those four counts together. That is the shape of nearly every Spark job: many tasks working on their own partitions in parallel, then a step that brings their results together.

First, a small tidy-up: the session builder moved into its own file, session dot py, so every job starts Spark the same way with one line. Now, an experiment. Lazy dot py counts the jobs Spark has run after each line. Reading October costs one job, the small one we saw that reads the header. Filtering to paid orders: still one job. Filtering again to German orders, and keeping two columns: still one. Those lines returned instantly, and no data was touched. Then count, and the number jumps to three: the counting ran as the two jobs we met in the last section, and found three hundred and seventy five paid German orders. This is the most important idea in Spark. There are two kinds of method. A transformation, like filter, select or group by, returns a new DataFrame at once. It does not compute anything. It only adds a step to a plan. An action, like count, show or write, asks for an answer, and that is when Spark runs a job. So a DataFrame is not data in memory, it is a description of how to get the data. Why work this way? Because when the action arrives, Spark sees the whole plan at once, and can optimise it: it can read only the two columns we kept, and drop rows as early as possible. Course four looks inside that optimiser. For now, the rule is simple: nothing runs until you ask for a result.

Now the first question the business actually asked: how much did we sell each day in October? Daily revenue dot py reads the month, keeps the paid orders, and groups them by day. To date turns each timestamp into its calendar day. For each day it counts the orders, and sums the totals. The totals are strings, so we cast them to a decimal with two places, an exact type for money. Order by day sorts the result. The terminal shows the first three days: forty four orders and five thousand one hundred and fifty one euros on the first of October. The side pane follows the job. Reading and filtering happen inside each partition, independently. Grouping is different: all of one day's orders must end up in the same place to be added up, and they start out scattered across partitions. So Spark moves rows between tasks. That move is called a shuffle, and Course five is about why it is the expensive part. The last line writes the result as CSV, and here is a surprise: out slash daily revenue is a folder, not a file. Spark writes in parallel, one file per partition, so every write produces a folder of part files. The underscore success file is empty, and only says the write finished. This time there is a single part file, with a header and thirty one days, because Spark noticed the result was tiny and merged its partitions before writing. On a bigger job you would see many part files, written at the same time. That is our first useful output: revenue per day, computed by Spark.

Things will go wrong, and in Spark they go wrong in two different places. This script makes both mistakes on purpose. The first selects a column called totl, a typo. It fails immediately, on the select line, before any job has run: an analysis exception. While building the plan, the driver checks every name against the data's columns, and Spark even suggests the column we probably meant, total. The second mistake is subtler. We cast the total to an integer, to get whole euros. That line runs without complaint, because it is a transformation, and nothing has been computed. The error only appears at show, when a task actually meets a total with cents, which is not a whole number. Spark four is strict here: rather than quietly dropping the cents, or returning nothing, it stops the job. So, a wrong name fails as you write the line. A wrong value fails only when a task reaches it, possibly after a long job has been running for an hour. Notice how both errors are reported. Each one names a condition, in capitals: unresolved column, and cast invalid input. That condition is the thing to search for, in the documentation or anywhere else. The terminal stayed readable, because the full details, including the failed task's stack trace, went to logs slash spark dot log, where grep finds them. With a working session, a first real job, and a way to read its failures, Course three starts on the real problem: Shopwave's data, from every source, with all its flaws.

Course three lands every Shopwave source in the lake, and it starts with types. First, the project grows up: the session moves into a package called shopwave, and the experiments of each section live in an explore folder. Course two left every column a string. There are two ways out. The quick one is infer schema: Spark reads the data and guesses each column's type. The other is to declare the types ourselves, and schemas dot py does that for the orders. The order id is a long, the timestamp a timestamp, and the total a decimal with two places, which the file calls money. The experiment reads October both ways. Guessing cost two jobs before we had asked a single question: one to read the header, and one to scan every file just to guess. On a year of data, that scan is not free. The declared read ran no jobs at all. Then the types. Spark guessed an integer for the order id, which will overflow one day, and a double for the total. A double is a binary fraction, and most amounts in cents cannot be stored exactly. Summing October's revenue per day, twenty one of thirty one days came out a hair off, like this one, five thousand six hundred and fifty six point one two nine nine nine and so on. The decimal sum is exactly five thousand six hundred and fifty six point one three. A finance team will notice the difference. So from now on, every source the platform reads has a declared schema, in one file, and money is always a decimal.

The warehouse sends a monthly file of returns, and it is the messiest source Shopwave has. Read it the default way, as U T F eight, and a German reason, Größe falsch, wrong size, comes out with question marks where the o umlaut and the sharp s should be. The warehouse's system writes Latin one, where each of those letters is a single byte that U T F eight cannot decode. Telling Spark the encoding fixes it, and the bronze returns function does exactly that. The second problem is lines that do not fit the schema. Spark's CSV reader has three modes. Fail fast stops at the first bad line. Drop malformed throws bad lines away without a word, which is how data quietly goes missing. Permissive, the default, keeps every line, and when we add a column called underscore corrupt record to the schema, Spark puts the whole raw line there whenever it cannot parse it. The function caches the result, because Spark refuses a query that looks only at the corrupt record column straight from the file, and then splits it in two: good rows, and bad rows. October has fifty eight good lines and three bad ones, and the side pane shows why each is bad. One is missing fields. One opens a quote and never closes it, so the parser swallowed the rest of the line into the reason. One writes its date day first, with slashes. None of them is lost: they are set aside, to be shown to the warehouse team, while the good rows move on.

The website's tracker sends every click as a line of JSON, one folder per day, and this is where Spark starts to earn its keep: a year of clicks is far bigger than a year of orders. Each event is nested. Beside plain fields like its id, time and type, it holds a context, an object describing the device, browser and campaign, and a list of items, each with a product id, a quantity and a price. Schemas dot py now declares that shape as CLICKS. A struct type holds the context, and an array type of structs holds the items. The experiment reads one day both ways. Guessing finds the nesting by itself, but it reads the event time as a plain string, because JSON has no timestamp type, and the price as a double again. Declared, the time is a real timestamp and the price is money. With the schema in place, the first of October holds eight hundred and ninety seven events. Most are product views, then page views, then items added to a cart, and forty seven checkouts, each followed by a purchase. Nested data is not a problem to flatten away as fast as possible. Spark reads it natively, and a field inside a struct is reached with a dot, like context dot campaign. The list of items is the harder part: one event can carry several products, and to count what was bought, each item has to become a row of its own.

Turning a list into rows is what explode does. Selecting explode of items produces one row for every element of every event's list, with the event's other columns repeated beside it. The side pane follows one purchase. As an event, it is a single row with three items in its list. After explode, it is three rows, one per product, each with its quantity and price, and the same event id. That is the shape every product question needs: what sold, how many, at what price. The counts show the catch. The day has eight hundred and ninety seven events, but only six hundred and thirty eight carry any items, because a page view lists no products. Explode produced seven hundred and eighteen item rows, and the two hundred and fifty nine events with an empty list simply vanished. That is right when we are counting items, and wrong when we are counting events. Explode outer keeps them: every event with an empty list stays as a single row with a null item, giving nine hundred and seventy seven rows in total. Neither is a default to reach for without thinking. Ask which question the rows are for, then pick the function that keeps the right ones. The terminal's table also shows show truncating long values: the event ids are cut to eight characters, so they fit the screen.

Data changes shape when nobody is watching. On the first of June, the web team shipped a new tracker. It renamed context dot device to device type, and it added a field called consent. Nothing failed. The experiment reads the last day of May and the first of June together, letting Spark guess one schema for both, and counts each field per file. The May file has device for every event and no device type. The June file has the opposite, plus consent. Notice that the change follows the file, not the event time: a late event from May that arrived in June's folder is written the new way. Now imagine our declared schema had kept only the new name. Spark would read May without complaint, and every May device would be null, silently. A declared schema simply ignores a field it does not name. So the CLICKS schema now declares both names, and bronze dot clicks merges them. Coalesce takes the first value that is not null, device type, else device, writes it back into the context struct as device, and drops the other field. After that, the device is known for every one of the one thousand eight hundred and three events across both days. The habit to keep is this: when a source changes shape, the schema records both shapes, with a comment saying when the change happened, and the code that merges them lives in one place.

Customers and products do not arrive as files. They live in the shop's own database, PostgreSQL, so we read them directly. Compose dot yaml describes that database for Docker. Docker compose up starts PostgreSQL seventeen, and init dot sql creates the two tables and loads them from the generated data, so every run starts from the same state. The status check says it is running and healthy. Spark talks to databases through JDBC, which needs the database's own driver, a jar file. Jars dot txt lists its address on Maven Central, curl downloads it into the jars folder, and the session now hands every jar in that folder to Spark. Reading a table is one line, and by default it is one query: one partition, read by one task, however big the table. Bronze dot table does better. It asks the database for the smallest and largest key, then tells Spark to split that range into four strides, one query each. The experiment prints Spark's own partition list: four WHERE clauses, each covering about five hundred customers, and the first one also catches any null keys. Four tasks run the four queries at the same time. Two things to keep in mind: the key should be spread evenly, or one query does all the work, and each partition is a separate connection to a database that also serves the live shop. The types came from the database itself: a bigint id, and a real date for signup.

Bronze will not store CSV. Here is why, measured. This lab writes a year of orders as Parquet and runs the same queries against both formats, reading the bytes from the same stage metrics the Spark UI shows. On disk, the CSV year is three hundred and sixty five files and nine hundred thousand bytes. As Parquet, it is one file of three hundred and seventy eight thousand: compressed, and typed. On the left is why CSV is slow. It stores one line per row, so to read one column, Spark must read and parse every line. Asking for German orders, with two columns, read the entire nine hundred thousand bytes. Parquet stores each column in its own chunk. The same question touched only the order id, country and total chunks, seventy three thousand bytes, about a twelfth. The plan at the bottom shows how: the read schema lists just those three columns, and the filter on country was pushed down into the scan itself. Parquet also keeps the smallest and largest value of every chunk. Since the file was written in order id order, asking for orders below one thousand let the scan skip almost everything: under seven thousand bytes read, against the CSV's full nine hundred thousand again. Column pruning, filter pushdown and min max skipping are why every serious data lake stores columnar files, and why everything we land from now on is Parquet.

Everything comes together in bronze dot py's main function, which lands every source in the lake. Bronze is the first layer of three. It changes nothing in the data itself: it only fixes the format and the types. Each file-based reader now adds two columns: underscore source file, the name of the file a row came from, and underscore file date, the day in the file's path. When something looks wrong next month, those two columns say exactly where it came from. The four daily sources, orders, their lines, payments and clicks, are written as Parquet partitioned by file date, so each day gets its own folder, as the listing of the clicks table shows. A query for one day can then read only that day's folder. Returns, which arrive monthly, are written whole, and their bad lines go to a quarantine folder as JSON, readable by anyone. Customers and products come over JDBC, four queries each. The run prints what landed. One thousand five hundred and forty six orders with two thousand seven hundred and forty eight order lines, one thousand four hundred and eighty four payments, two thousand seven hundred click events across three days, fifty eight returns, two thousand customers and fifty products, plus three quarantined lines. Two of those numbers already disagree: there are more orders than payments. Some orders were cancelled, some were never paid, and some were paid twice. Finding and fixing that is the work of the silver layer, in Course four.

Bronze kept every source as it came. Silver is the next layer: the same data, made clean and consistent, so every later question starts from the same trustworthy tables. Silver dot py starts with the clicks, and it is one select. Each argument is a column expression. A plain string, like event id, just picks a column. F dot col of context dot device reaches into the struct and, with alias, gives the result a new name, device. A function like to date makes a new column out of an existing one: the event's calendar day. Thirteen expressions in, and the nested context has become four flat columns that any tool can read. Bronze had ten columns; silver has thirteen. An expression is not a value. Printed, it is only a description, is null, of context dot campaign, just like a DataFrame is only a plan. It is computed inside an action, for every row, by the executors. The terminal shows the first clicks that came from a campaign, with their day and device. This style, one select listing every column of the output, is worth the extra lines: a reader sees the whole shape of the silver table in one place, and nothing sneaks in from upstream. Silver tables are what analysts, dashboards and the rest of this course will read, so their columns are chosen on purpose, one by one.

An anonymous visitor has no user id. Spark stores that as null: not zero, not empty, but unknown. And unknown behaves strangely in comparisons. The experiment counts October's thirty one thousand and forty six events. Eleven thousand three hundred and ninety seven have a null user id. Twenty one belong to customer two three nine. So how many do not belong to customer two three nine? Equals not, says nineteen thousand six hundred and twenty eight. Add the twenty one, and you get nineteen thousand six hundred and forty nine, not thirty one thousand. The anonymous events vanished from both answers. A comparison with null is itself null, unknown, and a filter keeps only rows where the condition is true. Is that event from customer two three nine? Unknown, so it is dropped, either way. When nulls should count as not equal, the null safe operator says so: not, user id null safe equals two three nine, keeps all thirty one thousand and twenty five. Silver also stops passing the problem on. A new column, visitor, uses coalesce, which returns its first argument that is not null: the customer's id when they are logged in, otherwise the browser's anonymous id. Every event now has a visitor. And when otherwise, Spark's if then else, labels each event as from a customer, or anonymous. The rule of thumb: decide what null means for each column once, in silver, and never let a query downstream rediscover it.

The website's tracker is built to never lose an event. When it is not sure an event arrived, it sends it again, which means some events arrive twice. This is called at least once delivery, and it is how almost every event pipeline behaves. In October's bronze clicks there are thirty one thousand and forty six rows, but only thirty thousand nine hundred and one distinct event ids. One hundred and forty five events were sent twice. Counted as they are, every page view, every cart and every purchase number would be slightly inflated, and nobody would know why. The fix is one call at the top of silver dot clicks: drop duplicates on event id. Spark groups the rows that share an id, which means rows from different partitions must meet, so like a group by, it is a shuffle. Then it keeps one row for each id. Silver now holds exactly thirty thousand nine hundred and one events. Be careful about which copy survives. Drop duplicates keeps whichever row it meets first, and makes no promise about which one. For exact copies of the same event, that does not matter. It matters a lot when the duplicates differ: an order paid twice has two different payments, with different ids and times, and picking one at random is wrong. That needs a window function, to keep the first by time, and windows are Course six.

On which day was an order placed? It sounds trivial, until the customers live in thirteen countries. Every timestamp in this platform is stored in UTC, one universal clock, and the session pins Spark to UTC too, so a time never shifts depending on whose laptop runs the job. But the business asks about days, and a German customer's Saturday starts two hours before UTC's does. Silver dot orders keeps both. Order date is the UTC day. For the local date, a map from country to time zone, built with create map, picks the zone for each row, from UTC timestamp converts the instant to that zone's clock, and to date takes the day. The experiment shows the difference. Ninety three of October's one thousand five hundred and forty six orders fall on a different day locally. This German order was placed at twenty two twenty two UTC, which in Berlin is already twenty past midnight on the next day. Customers in India, four and a half hours ahead of Berlin, often cross midnight too. And a customer in New York, at half past three in the morning UTC, was still on the previous evening. Which one is right? Both: finance closes its books in UTC, while marketing measuring a Black Friday in Berlin wants the German day. Silver keeps the instant and both days, so nobody has to redo the conversion, and nobody does it slightly differently.

Something in October's clicks is not human. To find it, we need a rule Spark does not have built in: does the user agent look like a bot, a crawler, a spider or a scraper? A user defined function, or UDF, lets us write that rule in plain Python. Is bot takes a user agent string, runs a regular expression over it, and returns true or false. The decorator tells Spark the result is a boolean, and silver dot clicks calls it like any other function, to make a new column. The result is striking. Two thousand four hundred and seventy seven events, eight percent of October, are bots, and they all come from one visitor, an anonymous id ten times busier than our most active customer. Its user agent openly says Shopwave Scraper. Left in, it would inflate page views, wreck the conversion funnel, and later dominate any per visitor computation. But look at what the UDF costs. Spark's executors are Java processes, and Python cannot run inside them. So every row's user agent is shipped out of the JVM to a separate Python worker process, the function runs there, and the answer is shipped back. The plan shows it as a step called batch eval Python, and in this plan it appears twice, once for the filter and once for the column. Spark cannot look inside a Python function either, so it cannot optimise it. The next section measures what that costs, and how to avoid it.

How much does leaving the JVM cost? This experiment applies the bot rule three ways to three million user agents: October's clicks, repeated a hundred times. First, pandas and pyarrow join the requirements, for a pandas UDF. Each version runs once to warm up, then is timed. The built in version uses r like, Spark's own regular expression match, which runs inside the JVM. The pandas UDF receives whole columns at a time, as pandas series, so Python is called once per batch of ten thousand rows instead of once per row. The plain Python UDF is the one from the last section. All three find the same two hundred and forty nine thousand bots. The built in version is clearly the fastest: about twice as fast as either UDF. The surprise is that the pandas UDF and the plain UDF take about the same time. In older versions of Spark, plain Python UDFs were dramatically slower, because rows crossed to Python one at a time. Spark four point two sends plain Python UDFs in Arrow batches too, which the terminal confirms is switched on, so the gap has closed. The lesson stays the same. Every UDF pays to move data out of the JVM and back, and hides its logic from the optimiser. So first look for a built in function: Spark has hundreds, for strings, dates, arrays and maps. Silver dot clicks now detects bots with r like, and the Python UDF is gone. Reach for a UDF only for logic that truly has no built in equivalent.

Why does writing order not matter much in Spark? Because the code is not run as written. This lab builds German revenue in cents the clumsy way queries really grow: a column computed before it is needed, multiplied by ten times ten, and two filters in two different places, then asks Spark to explain every stage of planning. The first box is the analyzed plan: our code, with every name checked against the data, bottom to top. Read from the relation up: project all eight columns plus cents, filter on status, project three columns, filter on country, aggregate. Then Catalyst, Spark's optimiser, rewrites it with rules, and the second box is the result. The two filters have merged into one and moved straight onto the relation. Ten times ten has become one hundred. And only the columns the answer needs survive. The table on the right lists the rules that actually changed the plan, taken from Spark's own rule metrics. Column pruning dropped the unused columns. Push down predicates moved the filters toward the data. Collapse project merged the selects. Constant folding computed ten times ten once, instead of for every row. And infer filters from constraints added is not null checks that let the scan skip rows early. The third box is the physical plan: the operators that actually run as tasks. The file scan reads just three columns and receives the filters, a partial aggregate runs in each task, an exchange shuffles by country, and a final aggregate adds up. This is also why built in functions beat UDFs: Catalyst can only optimise what it can see.

A job that runs without errors can still produce wrong data. A source sends half a file, a join silently drops rows, a column fills with nulls. Silver dot py's main function therefore never writes blindly. It builds every silver table, then passes the important ones through a gate, in quality dot py. A gate counts the rows that came in and the rows that came out, and checks that key columns, like the order id, the timestamp, the total and the visitor, have no nulls at all. If cleaning dropped more than a set share of the rows, or a key column has a null, the gate fails. Two percent is the default, because removing duplicates legitimately drops about half a percent. The first run passes. Orders lose nothing, and clicks lose the one hundred and forty five duplicates, under half a percent, so all seven silver tables are written. The second run shows a gate doing its job. With the limit tightened to a tenth of a percent through an environment variable, the clicks gate fails, the job prints that nothing was written, and exits with code one. That exit code is the important part. A scheduler running these jobs every night stops at a failed step, so a broken silver table never reaches gold or a dashboard. Silver is now complete: clean, typed, deduplicated, with visitors, local days and bots identified. Course five builds the gold layer on top of it, and meets the most expensive operation in Spark.

Silver is clean, but it is still shaped like the systems that produced it. Gold is shaped like the questions the business asks, and the classic shape is a star. At its centre is a fact table: one row for each thing that happened, here one row per order line, with the numbers you add up. Around it are dimensions: one row per thing you describe, customers and products. Gold dot py builds them. Fact sales joins each order line to its order, to get the date, the customer and the country, and computes revenue as quantity times unit price. The two dimensions are simple selects. The course's data now runs through the end of November, so it includes Black Friday. The experiment builds the star and checks it. Seven thousand three hundred and eighty nine order lines, two thousand customers, fifty products. Then the most important line in this section: paid revenue summed from the lines, and paid revenue summed from the orders' totals, must agree to the cent. They do, four hundred and fifty eight thousand three hundred and eighty eight euros and eighty nine cents both ways. A check like that catches a join that silently duplicates or loses rows. Joining the fact to the product dimension answers the first real question: electronics sells the most, then beauty. Every one of these answers needed a join, and joins are where Spark spends its effort. The rest of this course is about what a join really costs, and what Black Friday does to it.

A join pairs rows from two tables on a key, but which rows survive depends on the kind of join, and choosing the wrong one quietly changes answers. The experiment joins Shopwave's orders that were not cancelled, four thousand one hundred of them, to the payment provider's four thousand and sixty eight payments, on order id. An inner join keeps only pairs that match: four thousand and sixty eight rows. A left join keeps every order, with its payment if there is one, or nulls if not: four thousand one hundred and twelve rows. Why more rows than orders? Because twelve orders were paid twice, and a join pairs each order with every matching payment. That is the classic way joins inflate revenue. Then two joins that people often forget. A left semi join keeps the orders that have a payment, without adding any payment columns, and without duplicating anything: four thousand and fifty six. And a left anti join keeps the orders that have no payment at all: forty four orders, placed and never paid. One line of code finds money the shop is owed. Here are the first three. Semi and anti joins answer exists and does not exist questions, which in SQL you would write with exists or not in. Use them instead of a left join followed by a null filter: they say what you mean, never duplicate rows, and Spark can execute them more cheaply.

Every join and every group by in Spark rests on one operation, the shuffle, and this lab shows it from Spark's own metrics. The query is revenue by country over the fact table. It runs as two stages. In the first, four map tasks each read their own partition of the order lines, seven thousand three hundred and eighty nine rows between them, and each one sums revenue per country, but only for the rows it holds. Each task then writes its partial sums to shuffle files on local disk, sorted into partitions by a hash of the country, so that every partial sum for Germany, from every task, lands in the same partition. Here that is only fifty two rows, a few hundred bytes per task, because the sums were combined before writing. That is a stage boundary. No task of the next stage can start until every map task has finished writing, because any of them might hold part of Germany's answer. In the second stage, reduce tasks read their partitions across the network and add the partial sums together into thirteen country totals. There are two hundred shuffle partitions by default, but adaptive query execution saw how little data there was and gave them all to a single task. The table at the bottom is the stage table the Spark UI shows. Shuffles are the expensive part of Spark: disk writes, network reads, and a barrier where the whole job waits for its slowest task. Most of Spark tuning is about shuffling less, or shuffling evenly.

How does Spark join two big tables? This experiment joins order lines to orders, and first switches off broadcasting, which our small month would otherwise use, so we see the join Spark uses when both sides are large: the sort merge join. The plan, printed by the script and drawn on the right, reads from the bottom. Each side is scanned, then goes through an exchange, which is a shuffle on order id: every row is sent to the task that owns its order id's partition. So order lines and orders with the same id meet in the same task. Each side is then sorted by order id. And finally the merge join walks the two sorted lists together, like merging two sorted decks of cards, emitting every matching pair in a single pass. It needs no table to fit in memory, which is why it works at any size and is Spark's default for large joins. The cost is in the exchanges. Both sides cross the shuffle in full: one hundred and sixty thousand bytes here for seven thousand rows, and on a real year, gigabytes. The same join will be needed again and again, so it is worth asking whether one side could avoid moving at all. When one side is small, it can.

Payments arrive in four currencies, and the business wants every amount in euros. The finance team's exchange rates are a new source: bronze now lands them, one row per day and currency, a little over a thousand rows. Gold's fact payments joins each payment to the rate for its day and currency, and divides. Euro payments have no rate row, so the join is a left join, and a missing rate counts as one. The rates table is tiny, so instead of shuffling both sides, Spark can broadcast it: the driver collects the whole table once and sends a copy to every task. Each task then joins its own payments against its local copy, and the payments never move. The experiment runs the same join both ways. Forced into a sort merge join, thirty nine thousand five hundred bytes cross the shuffle. Broadcast, two hundred and thirty six bytes, and those belong to the final count, not to the join. On a real year of payments that is the difference between moving gigabytes and moving nothing. The plan names it a broadcast hash join. Spark broadcasts on its own when one side is under ten megabytes, but gold dot py says so explicitly with F dot broadcast, because the rule depends on Spark's size estimate, and the fact payments table should never fall back to a shuffle by accident. Every payment now has an amount in euros: four hundred and eighty eight thousand euros in all.

How many tasks does a shuffle use? Whatever spark dot sql dot shuffle dot partitions says, and the default is two hundred. The experiment switches off adaptive execution, to see Spark's raw behaviour, and groups October and November's sales by day. Sixty one days of results, and two hundred tasks to compute them, but only fifty five of those tasks received any rows at all. The other one hundred and forty five were scheduled, started and finished with nothing to do. Two hundred is a sensible number for gigabytes of data. For a month, it is mostly overhead. Set it to eight, and the same query runs as eight tasks, all of them busy. The number of partitions also decides the number of files a write produces, one per partition. To change it before writing there are two tools. Coalesce, to a smaller number, merges neighbouring partitions without a shuffle, which is cheap but can leave uneven sizes: coalesce one wrote a single file. Repartition does a full shuffle and produces partitions of even size, more or fewer: repartition four wrote four files. A note on the code: the query is built again after changing the setting, because a DataFrame keeps the plan it made the first time it ran. Choosing these numbers by hand for every job does not scale, and the right number changes as data grows. Two sections from now, Spark picks it while the job runs.

Shopwave has a bestseller. Product one is sixteen percent of all order lines, one thousand one hundred and fifty three of seven thousand three hundred and eighty nine. That is normal in retail, and it is a problem for joins. A shuffle sends every row with the same key to the same task, so when the fact table is joined to the product dimension, every sale of product one goes to one task. The experiment runs that join with adaptive execution off, and reads every task's row count from the task metrics. To make sure Spark computes every column, it uses a no op write, which runs the whole query and writes nothing: a plain count would let Spark skip all but the product id, and measure almost nothing. The plot shows the largest six tasks and the median. The largest task read one thousand one hundred and fifty four rows, the bestseller; the median task read eighty four. That is fourteen times the typical work. Here it costs milliseconds. On a real Black Friday, with millions of lines, that one task runs for minutes while every other task is finished and idle, and the stage cannot end until it does. This is data skew, and it is the most common reason a Spark job that ran fine yesterday is slow today. Adding machines does not help: one key always lands in one task. The fix has to split the hot key.

Adaptive query execution, AQE, lets Spark change its plan while a job runs, once the real sizes are known. A shuffle is a natural checkpoint: when a stage finishes, Spark knows exactly how many bytes landed in every partition, and it can re-plan the next stage with facts instead of estimates. AQE does three things with them. It merges partitions that are too small, so there are no empty tasks. It splits a partition that is far bigger than the rest, so a skewed join is shared out. And it can switch a sort merge join to a broadcast, if one side turned out to be small. That last one is switched off here, to watch the skew handling on its own. AQE's thresholds are sized for real data, where a partition counts as skewed above two hundred and fifty six megabytes. Our month is tiny, so the script scales the thresholds down to kilobytes. The rules are the same; only the numbers are smaller. Then the skewed join from the last section runs twice. With AQE off: two hundred tasks, the largest one thousand one hundred and fifty four rows. With AQE on: thirteen tasks, and the largest is eight hundred and nineteen rows, because the bestseller's partition was cut into pieces. Notice that the join read two more rows with AQE on. That is the proof of the split: product one's single dimension row was copied to each extra piece, so each piece can still be joined. AQE has been on by default since Spark three point two, which is one more reason to stay on a current version.

Adaptive execution cannot always help. It might be switched off on an older cluster, or the join might be a kind it cannot split, such as a full outer join. The manual technique is called salting. The idea: make the hot key into several keys. Each sale gets a salt, a number from zero to seven, computed from a hash of its order id and line, so it is the same on every run. The product dimension is copied eight times, once for each salt value. Then the join is on the product id and the salt together. Product one, which was a single key going to one task, is now eight keys, product one with salt zero up to product one with salt seven, spread over eight tasks. With AQE off, the plain join has forty four busy tasks, and the largest reads one thousand one hundred and fifty four rows. The salted join has one hundred and seventy nine busy tasks, and its largest reads three hundred and twenty nine. The work is spread far more evenly. Salting has a price. The small side is copied once per salt value, so it grows eight times, and the code is harder to read: the next person to see that salt column needs a comment explaining it. Reach for salting only when a skewed join is still slow with AQE on. Gold is now complete: a star schema, payments in euros, and the tools to keep joins fast when the data is uneven. Course six puts it to work answering the business's questions.

With gold in place, the platform can finally answer the business, and from this course on the data covers all of twenty twenty six. The first answers are the key performance indicators, KPIs, per day. Daily KPIs in analytics dot py filters to paid order lines, groups by day, and computes three numbers. Orders, counted as distinct order ids, because an order has several lines. Gross merchandise value, GMV, the sum of revenue. And average order value, GMV divided by orders. The script also writes the result to a small CSV, and the chart on the right draws it: every point is a real day. The year: three hundred and sixty five days, eighteen thousand and fourteen paid orders, two point one eight million euros of GMV, and an average order of about one hundred and twenty one euros. A typical day brings in about five and a half thousand euros. Then there is the spike. On Black Friday, Shopwave took eight hundred and thirty seven orders and ninety eight thousand euros, eighteen times a median day, and the Monday after was the second biggest day of the year. That spike is why the platform has to be built for its peak, not its average. One detail matters: the result is three hundred and sixty five rows, small enough to bring to the driver with to pandas. That is the usual shape of analytics in Spark: process billions of rows on the cluster, and bring back only the small answer.

Which three products sell best in each category? A group by cannot answer that alone, because grouping by category collapses each category to one row, and the products disappear. This needs a window function. Top products first adds up revenue per product, and joins the product dimension to get each one's name and category. Then it defines a window: partition by category, order by revenue, descending. Partition by splits the rows into one group per category, like a group by, but nothing is collapsed: every product row stays. Order by sorts the rows inside each group. Rank, computed over that window, numbers them: one for the best seller in its category, two for the next, and so on. Filtering to ranks up to three leaves eighteen rows, three per category, and the terminal lists them: perfume leads beauty, a thriller leads books, headphones lead electronics. Under the hood, a window is computed by shuffling the rows so each partition lands in one task, then sorting inside it. That is the same shuffle as a group by, so the same lessons about skew apply. Rank, dense rank and row number differ only in how they treat ties. Rank leaves gaps after a tie, dense rank does not, and row number breaks ties arbitrarily, which is exactly what the payments deduplication needed back in Course four.

Daily GMV is noisy: weekends are busier, and one big day hides the trend. A seven day moving average smooths it, and a window can compute it with a frame: for each row, which neighbouring rows to include. Moving average orders all the days in time, and uses range between minus six and zero: the current day and the six before it. The chart shows the result. The grey line is the raw daily GMV, the blue line its seven day average, which climbs smoothly into December and carries Black Friday's spike for exactly a week. The experiment then shows the one detail that trips people up. There are two kinds of frame. Rows between counts rows. Range between counts values of the order by column, here days. When every day is present, they agree. So the script removes the twenty sixth of November and compares them. On the twenty fifth, both averages are identical. From the twenty seventh, they differ. Rows between still takes the last seven rows, which now reach back eight calendar days. Range between still takes exactly the last seven days, and simply has one row fewer in them. For anything measured in time, use range, ordered by a number of days or seconds: it is what the question means. One warning: this window has no partition by, so all three hundred and sixty five rows go to a single task. For a year of days that is fine; Spark logs a warning, because for millions of rows it would not be.

The clickstream records events, but marketing thinks in visits: someone arrives, browses, maybe buys, and leaves. There is no visit id in the data, so we build one. This is called sessionization, and it is a classic job for window functions. Sessions partitions the events by visitor, in time order. Lag gives each event the time of the one before it. If there is no previous event, or the gap is more than thirty minutes, this event starts a new session, marked with a one, otherwise a zero. Then a running sum of those ones, over all the visitor's events so far, numbers the sessions: one, one, one, then two after a long gap. Visitor one, on the right, shows it. Four events within a few minutes on the second of October form session one; the next afternoon's visit is session two. October holds about twenty seven thousand events from four thousand people, cut into six thousand one hundred and seventy sessions, about four events each. The bot is different. Its two thousand three hundred events come in four hundred and one sessions, all from one visitor, which means one task in the window computes them all. That is the skew from Course five again, now inside a window instead of a join, and windows have no adaptive split. Every later question about visits, funnels and attribution builds on these session ids.

Of everyone who visits Shopwave, how many buy? A funnel answers it step by step: viewed a page, viewed a product, added to cart, checked out, purchased. Funnel works on the sessions from the last section, leaving out the bot, whose visits never buy and would only drag every rate down. For each session it records, step by step, whether the session reached it: the maximum of a zero or one per event. Then it adds those up across all sessions. The chart and the table show October. Six thousand one hundred and sixty six visits viewed a page, and almost all of them viewed a product. Then the biggest drop: only sixty one percent added anything to a cart. A quarter of all visits reached checkout, and a quarter bought. So Shopwave converts one visit in four, and the place to improve is between looking at a product and putting it in the cart. Look closely and there is one more purchase than checkout. One session recorded a purchase without its checkout event, perhaps a click the tracker lost. Real data has rough edges like that, and a funnel should be read as a picture of behaviour, not an accounting identity. Notice too that this whole computation is one group by over sessions, then one aggregate: nothing here needed a loop over visitors, even though the question is about each visitor's path.

A shop lives on customers who come back. Cohort retention measures it: group customers by the month of their first order, their cohort, then ask what share of each cohort ordered again one, two, three months later. Cohorts takes three steps. First, a window over each customer's orders finds the earliest month: that is their cohort. Second, months between gives each order's age, the number of months since the cohort month. Third, a pivot turns ages into columns, counting distinct customers in each cell, and dividing by the cohort's size in month zero. The table reads row by row. January's cohort is the largest, nine hundred and five customers, partly because the data starts in January, so everyone who was already a customer appears new then. Around half of them order again in every later month. Later cohorts are smaller, and come back somewhat less, between thirty and forty percent a month. Pivot is the step worth noticing. It turns rows into columns, which is how a spreadsheet person expects to read this, and passing the list of ages explicitly, zero to eleven, saves Spark a pass over the data to find the distinct values. Cohort tables are where retention problems show up first: a new marketing channel bringing customers who never return looks fine in daily KPIs, and terrible here.

Marketing wants to treat customers differently, and the simplest serious way to group them is RFM. Recency: how many days since their last order. Frequency: how many orders. Monetary: how much they have spent. RFM computes the three per customer, as of the end of the year, then scores each from one to four with n tile, which splits the customers into four equal groups. For recency fewer days is better, so it is ordered descending. A segment then follows from the scores: champions are the most recent and most frequent, loyal customers order often, new ones are recent but have ordered once or twice, and lost ones have not ordered for months. Everyone else is occasional. The result, for one thousand nine hundred and eighty four customers who paid this year. Loyal customers are the largest group and bring in the most money, over nine hundred thousand euros. Two hundred and twenty four champions average twenty eight orders each, with their last order six days ago. Four hundred and thirty one customers are lost: their last order was over four months ago, a list worth an email. As with the moving average, these windows have no partition by: every customer is sorted in one task to cut the quartiles. For two thousand customers that is instant. For ten million, it is the bottleneck, and the fix is approximate percentiles, computed in parallel.

Marketing spends money on campaigns and wants to know which ones bring sales. First, a new source: marketing's campaign list lands in bronze. It is a single JSON array spread over several lines, so it is read with multi line set to true; ordinary JSON reading expects one object per line. Attribution then credits each purchase with the last campaign its visitor came through in the same session. Last, with ignore nulls, over the session's events so far, carries the most recent campaign forward to every later event. Purchases then get their revenue, summed from their items inside the array, with aggregate, a higher order function that folds a list without exploding it. Finally, a join to the campaigns, but not on equality alone: the campaign must match, and the purchase date must fall between the campaign's start and end. That is a range join, and Spark handles it like any other join with a condition. October's answer: most sales came from no campaign at all, direct visits, one thousand one hundred and seventeen sales and one hundred and thirty six thousand euros. The newsletter brought two hundred and twenty two sales, retargeting two hundred and seven. The spring sale and Black Friday campaigns were not running in October, so the range condition gives them nothing, even if a click carried their name. Last touch is only one model, and a simple one, but it is a fair start, and it is all in one query.

Everything in this course could have been written in SQL. Spark SQL is not a separate system: it is another way into the same engine. The script registers the session DataFrame as a temporary view called visits, which gives it a name that SQL can use for the rest of this Spark session. Funnel dot sql is the funnel from section five, in plain SQL: a common table expression marks, per session, whether each step was reached, then the outer query adds them up. Spark dot sql runs it and returns an ordinary DataFrame. The two answers, from SQL and from the DataFrame code, are identical, step for step. And the last line of the terminal shows why: after Catalyst has optimised them, the two plans are the same plan. Both are parsed into the same logical operators, rewritten by the same rules, and run as the same tasks. So choosing between SQL and the DataFrame API is a question of who reads the code, not of speed. SQL is easier for analysts and for long declarative queries. Python is easier when logic is reused, tested, or built up in functions, like the sessions function this query depends on. Most real platforms mix them, exactly like this: Python builds the reusable datasets, and SQL asks the questions. Course seven turns to the tables themselves, and fixes a weakness the platform has had since Course three.

Gold is a set of folders of Parquet files, and every report reads them. Here is what happens when a nightly rebuild goes wrong. The script rebuilds the sales fact table in place, with mode overwrite, and plants the kind of bug real jobs have: a row from December raises an error. Before the job, the table holds thirty five thousand and forty three rows. The job starts, and the first thing an overwrite does is delete the old files, before a single new row exists. Then tasks start writing new part files, one of them reaches December, and the job fails. Spark cleans up the half written files, as it should. What is left is an empty folder. Reading the table now does not return old data or new data: it fails, because there is nothing to infer a schema from. And while the job was running, a dashboard reading the folder would have seen some new files and none of the old ones, a table that never existed. The root problem is that a folder has no idea which files make up the table. Whatever is in it, is the table. That is the problem Delta Lake solves, with a log that says which files are the table, written last.

A Delta table is two things in one folder: ordinary Parquet files, and a folder called underscore delta log. This lab writes the product dimension as a Delta table, then appends two rows, and looks at what is on disk. The log holds one JSON file per commit, numbered from zero. Commit zero carries a commit info action naming the operation, a metadata action with the table's schema, a protocol action, and one add action per data file, each with statistics: the row count, and the minimum and maximum of every column. Commit one is smaller: commit info, and one add for the new file. Reading the table means reading the log first, then exactly the files it adds, and no others. There are six Parquet files on disk but only five adds: the append's empty task still wrote a file with no rows, and no commit ever added it, so no reader ever sees it. The same is true of a file a failed job half wrote. A commit is a single file, created atomically: if two writers race for commit number two, only one of them can create it, and the other must retry. That one rule gives a folder of files transactions. And the statistics are why Delta can skip files without opening them, which comes back in Course eight.

Now the lake moves to Delta. PySpark needs two things for it: the delta spark package, whose version must match Spark's, in requirements, and its two jars in jars dot txt. The session gains two settings that switch on Delta's SQL commands and let the catalog know Delta tables. In gold, the change is one word per write: format delta. Then the experiment from section one runs again, the same bug, the same failing December row, against the Delta table. The job fails just as before, the error is a failed write task instead of the raised exception, but a reader afterwards still sees all thirty five thousand and forty three rows, and the history holds only version zero. Delta never deletes the old files during an overwrite: it writes new ones, and only a final commit swaps them in. The failed job never committed, so as far as any reader knows, it never happened. Tables that already exist as Parquet do not need rewriting. Convert to delta lists the files of bronze's orders, three hundred and sixty five of them, one per day, and writes a first commit that adds them all, in place. The same twenty thousand and twenty four rows, now a table with a history.

Until now every job rebuilt its tables from scratch. That stops working as the history grows, and gold orders is the first table to load incrementally. Lake dot py is a new module for the jobs that keep Delta tables up to date. Load orders reads the newest order date already in the table, the high water mark, and reads only the silver orders after it. The new rows are appended in one Delta commit. The first run, told to stop at the end of November, loads seventeen thousand nine hundred and forty four orders. The next run finds the mark at November the thirtieth, and adds December's two thousand and eighty. The third run finds nothing newer and adds nothing. That last run matters most. The mark is read from the table itself, inside the same transaction that moves it, so a job that crashed halfway, or was started twice by a scheduler, never loads a day twice. A mark kept anywhere else, in a file or a variable, can drift from the data it describes.

Orders do not stay paid. They ship, and then they are delivered, and the shop's database publishes every change as an event: a change data capture feed. A week of it is one thousand nine hundred and seventy six changes, and five hundred and thirty seven orders changed twice in that week, shipped one day and delivered a few days later. Merge is how Delta applies such a feed: match each source row to a target row by order id, and update the matched ones. Merged as it comes, the feed fails. Two source rows match the same order, and Delta refuses to guess which one wins. So latest keeps only the newest change per order, with row number over a window, and the merge also checks that the change is newer than what the table already holds, so an old event replayed late cannot undo a new one. The result: one thousand four hundred and thirty nine orders updated, in a single commit. Paid orders fall, shipped and delivered appear, and cancelled and placed orders are untouched. In a folder of Parquet, an update means rewriting the whole table. Merge rewrites only the files that hold matched rows.

Prices change, and a report on March must use March's prices. Overwriting the price in the product table, type one, forgets the old price. A slowly changing dimension of type two keeps a row for every price a product has had, each with the day it became valid and the day it stopped. Price history builds it from the price change file. Valid to is the day before the product's next price, found with lead over the product's rows in date order. The current price has no next price, so its valid to is the last day of year nine nine nine nine, an open end that keeps between working, and is current flags it. Sixty six rows, eight products repriced. Product ten had three prices this year, the last from the day after Black Friday. The check joins every sale to the price valid on the day it was sold: all thirty five thousand and forty three sales find their row, and not one has a price that disagrees. That join, a range join on dates, is how every as of question is answered.

Every Delta commit leaves the files of earlier versions where they were, and the log remembers which files each version had. That makes mistakes recoverable. Here is a classic one: a day's load written with mode overwrite instead of append. Gold orders goes from twenty thousand and twenty four orders to forty seven, one day's worth. The history shows it plainly: two appends, then an overwrite. Reading with version as of one returns the table exactly as it was before the bad load, all twenty thousand and twenty four orders, because those files are still on disk. Restore makes that version current again. It does not delete the mistake: it is a new commit, version three, so the history still shows what happened and when. Time travel also answers quieter questions, like what did this report read last Tuesday, as long as the old files have not been vacuumed away, which is the last section of this course.

A Delta table has a schema in its log, and every write is checked against it before anything is committed. The script appends two December orders three ways. First with the total as a string: refused, Delta cannot merge a string into a decimal column. Second with a new column, channel, that marketing has started sending: refused too, the write's schema does not match the table's. Third, the same write with merge schema set to true, a deliberate decision to evolve the table. It is written, and the table now has nine columns. The twenty thousand and twenty four older rows read the new column as null, without being rewritten, and the two new rows carry app. Compare a folder of Parquet: it accepts any write. The wrong type lands in new files, and the failure surfaces later, in the next reader, far from the job that caused it. Delta moves the failure to the writer, where it belongs.

A nightly job that appends one day at a time writes small files, and a table of many small files gets slow: a task opens its files one after another, and opening a file costs more than reading a small one. The script appends December's sales one day at a time, thirty one appends, and the table has thirty one files. Optimize compacts them: one commit removes the thirty one small files from the table and adds one file with the same rows. The table now has one file, but the disk still holds all thirty two, because older versions still need the small ones for time travel. Vacuum deletes the files no version within the retention period needs. The default retention is seven days; this demo sets it to zero, which a real table should never do while anything might still be reading it. Thirty seven files and folders deleted, and the rows are unchanged, three thousand six hundred and seventy two. On a large table, Delta's liquid clustering goes further, and keeps rows with similar keys in the same files, so the file statistics can skip more of them.

This course measures. The data grows to scale factor one: the whole year, two million orders and three and a half million order lines, about two hundred megabytes of exports. Scale dot py reads them straight from the CSV folders and joins every paid order to its lines. To see what a job does, Spark can write an event log: every job, stage and task as a line of JSON. That is the same record the Spark UI is drawn from, which is why this course never needs a screenshot of it. The script switches the log on, runs revenue by country over the year, stops Spark so the log is complete, and reads every completed stage back. Two stages of twelve tasks each read a CSV folder, the orders and the order lines, and shuffle every row out, because the join needs both sides partitioned by order id. The third stage reads more than five million shuffled rows, joins them, and writes just fifty two partial sums. The last stage, one task, adds them up. The seconds column is real and changes with every run: read it as a proportion, the file reading stages take most of the time. The rest of this course works through what to do about each part.

Most Spark failures at scale are about memory, so before tuning anything, here is where an executor's memory goes. In local mode the driver is also the executor, and by default it gets one gigabyte of heap. Spark first keeps three hundred megabytes for itself, always. Of the rest, forty percent is user memory: your own objects, and the data a Python or Scala function builds while it runs. The other sixty percent is unified memory, which Spark manages, and it is shared between two uses. Storage holds cached DataFrames and broadcast tables. Execution holds the working data of shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations. The boundary between them moves. Half of unified memory is storage's, protected; above that, execution can take memory back from storage by evicting cached blocks, because a running task matters more than a cache. When execution itself runs out, a task does not fail: it spills, writing what it holds to disk and reading it back later, which is the next section. User memory has no such escape hatch: too much there is an out of memory error. On a real cluster each executor also gets memory overhead outside the heap, ten percent or at least three hundred and eighty four megabytes, for the JVM itself and for Python workers. The lab reads every number here from the running JVM and Spark's own settings, and the last line is what the Spark UI would call storage memory: the whole unified pool.

When a task runs out of execution memory, it spills. This script sorts the whole year of order lines within eight partitions, twice. With Spark's memory as it is, every task's rows fit, and nothing spills. The second run squeezes each task, with an internal setting that forces a spill after a hundred thousand rows, the way a too small executor behaves on real volumes. Now every task fills its memory, writes a sorted run to disk, carries on, and merges the runs at the end. The stage metrics show two numbers for it. Spill in memory is the size the rows took as objects; spill on disk is the same rows serialized and compressed, much smaller. The result is identical: spill is slower, never wrong. In the Spark UI a stage with spill is the first place to look when a job is slow. The fixes, in order: give each task fewer rows, with more partitions; give it more memory; or give it less data, by filtering and selecting columns before the wide operation.

Three questions about the same year of sales: total revenue, lines per country, and how many lines have more than two items. Without a cache, each question reads both CSV folders and joins them again from scratch. With cache, the first action computes the joined data and keeps it in storage memory, and the next two read it from there. The timings show both sides of caching. The first cached question is no faster, often a little slower, because it also fills the cache. The next two are much faster. The cache itself holds two hundred partitions, the join's output, in memory, and nothing spilled to disk. So cache a DataFrame when several actions reuse it and it fits in storage memory. Do not cache something used once: that only costs memory. And call unpersist when you are done, or the cache holds memory that execution could have used.

How many tasks read a folder of files is decided before the job starts. At scale factor one, the order items are three hundred and sixty five files, seventy megabytes, about two hundred kilobytes each. Spark packs files into input partitions of up to max partition bytes, a hundred and twenty eight megabytes by default. But it also charges every file an open cost of four megabytes, because opening a file is not free. Three hundred and sixty five files times four megabytes is a lot of pretend data, so the default gives twelve partitions, not one. At sixteen megabytes, ninety two. At one megabyte, smaller than a single file plus its open cost, every file gets at least one partition: three hundred and sixty nine. The usual target is around a hundred and twenty eight megabytes of real data per task, and a few tasks per core. Too few partitions leave cores idle; too many spend their time starting tasks and opening files. When a table is many small files, the fix is not a setting. It is compacting the files, as optimize did in the lakehouse course.

The same question two ways: how many orders came from Germany. The year is written as Parquet, sorted by country, so each file's minimum and maximum say which countries it holds. Written as a built in comparison, the filter appears in the plan as a pushed filter: the Parquet reader checks each file's statistics and reads only where Germany can be. Four hundred and eighty eight thousand rows read, exactly the answer. Written as a Python UDF, the filter is a black box. Spark cannot see that it compares country to a constant, so nothing is pushed, every one of the two million rows is read, and each is sent to a Python worker to be tested. The answer is identical. The work is four times bigger before the Python cost is even counted. One more thing surfaced while building this step: Spark four's default Arrow batched UDFs stalled on this scan, so the script uses the row at a time kind. Either way, the habit to take from here is to read the plan, the pushed filters and the columns read, whenever a query reads more than it should, and to keep filters in built in functions Spark can see.

Delta keeps the same kind of statistics in its log: for every file, the minimum and maximum of its columns, written with every add action. The script writes the year of sales as a Delta table of forty eight files, with repartition by range on the order date, so each file holds a short run of days, about four files a month. Then it asks for one day, Black Friday: a hundred and forty seven thousand and eighty nine lines. Delta compares the day with each file's range before Spark plans a single task, and opens one file. Forty seven are skipped without being read. This only works when a file covers a narrow range of the column you filter on. Written in random order, every file would hold the whole year, and every file would be read. That is what Delta's clustering, and Z ordering before it, are for: they keep similar values together so the statistics can skip.

The last measurement in this course: the same job, revenue by country over the year, on one, two, three and four cores. Each run is its own process, and each one runs the query once to warm up the JVM before timing the second run. The machine has four CPUs. Two cores are clearly faster than one, but not twice as fast, and every core added after that buys less. The plot shows the measured speed up against the perfect diagonal, and the gap grows. Some work does not split: planning the query, starting tasks, the final reduce that adds up a few dozen partial sums. And the cores share one disk, one memory bus and one operating system. This is Amdahl's law, and a cluster obeys it too, where the network and the shuffle are the shared parts. Adding executors is the last resort, not the first: measure where the time goes, as this course did, and fix that.

Until now the clickstream arrived as files, an hour at a time, and every number on the dashboard was a day old. Marketing wants it live. The platform's front door for live data is Kafka, added to compose dot yaml as a single broker. Kafka stores records in topics, and a topic is a log: records are appended, kept for days, and read by as many consumers as like, each at its own pace. A topic is split into partitions so that it can be written and read in parallel. Clicks has four. The tracker, which used to write JSON files, now publishes each event as a record, with the visitor as its key. Kafka hashes the key to choose the partition, so every event of one visitor lands in the same partition, in the order it happened. One day of October is eight hundred and ninety seven events. Kafka's own tool shows where each partition ends: two hundred and eighty nine records in partition zero, down to a hundred and eighty five in partition one. Those positions are offsets, and offsets are how Spark will keep track of what it has read.

Reading Kafka from Spark looks almost exactly like reading files: read stream instead of read, format Kafka, the broker's address and the topic, starting from the earliest offset. What comes back is a streaming DataFrame, and the session confirms it: is streaming is true. Each row is a Kafka record: a key and a value as raw bytes, the topic, the partition and the offset. Kafka stores no types, so the value is just the bytes the tracker sent. From JSON parses them with the clicks schema from the bronze course, the same one the files used, and the event's fields become columns again, with partition and offset kept alongside. A stream needs somewhere to go and a trigger. Here the sink is a memory table, for looking at, and the trigger is available now: read everything in the topic, then stop. All eight hundred and ninety seven events arrive, spread over the four partitions exactly as Kafka reported. The point of this design is that the same DataFrame code, select, filter, group by, now runs on data that keeps arriving.

How does Spark run a query on data that never ends? It does not, quite: it runs a series of small batch jobs, called micro batches. This lab limits each batch to three hundred records and reads its own progress reports. Each batch starts with a trigger: Spark looks at the end offsets in every partition and plans a range, no more than three hundred records, spread across the partitions in proportion. Before running anything, it writes that range to the checkpoint, in a file named after the batch number under offsets. Then the batch runs, as an ordinary Spark job over exactly that range. When the sink has the results, Spark writes a matching file under commits. Here that is four batches: two hundred and ninety eight records, two hundred and ninety nine, two hundred and ninety nine, and the last single record. Offsets and commits each hold four files, zero to three. That pair of folders is the whole trick. If the query stops, a restart reads the checkpoint, finds the last batch that was planned but not committed, and runs exactly that range again.

Here is that restart for real. To delta streams the events into a Delta table, with a checkpoint. The first run carries a bug that fails on one event in the second batch. The stream stops with stream failed. The table holds only the first batch, two hundred and ninety eight events. The second batch was planned, its offsets written, but never committed.
