The bug is fixed and the same query starts again. It reads the checkpoint, sees batch one was never committed, and runs it again over exactly the same range, because Kafka still holds those records. Could batch zero be written twice? No: Delta records the stream's batch ids in its own log, so a batch that was already committed is skipped. Checkpoint plus a transactional sink is exactly once. The table ends with all eight hundred and ninety seven events. But only eight hundred and ninety three distinct ids: four events were sent twice by the tracker itself. Exactly once means each Kafka record is written once; duplicates the source sent are the job of section seven.

Now the number marketing asked for: revenue per hour, live. Purchases keeps purchase events and adds their basket's value. Revenue per groups them by a window of event time, one hour wide. Window is a function of a timestamp: a purchase at fifteen forty two belongs to the window from fifteen hundred to sixteen hundred. These are tumbling windows, one after another with no overlap, so every event lands in exactly one. It is event time, when the purchase happened, not when the record reached Kafka. Each window's count and sum live in Spark's state store, and every batch that brings purchases for a window updates it. In complete mode the whole result table is written after every batch. After four batches, the day has sixteen hours with sales, and the busiest was three to four in the afternoon. Complete mode has a cost: every window ever seen stays in state, for ever. For one day that is nothing. For a stream that runs for months, windows must be allowed to close, which is what watermarks are for.

Events arrive late. The tracker buffers on a phone with no signal, and one percent of Shopwave's events land hours or days after they happened. So when is the count for ten o'clock final? A watermark answers that. With event time and a delay of two hours, Spark tracks the latest event time it has seen, and the watermark is that minus two hours. A window that ends before the watermark is final: in append mode it is written once, and its state is freed. An event older than the watermark arrives too late: its window is already written, so the event is dropped. This lab counts events per hour over three days of clicks. Eight batches; seventy five hours written as final, holding two thousand eight hundred and ninety eight events. Eight events arrived later than two hours and were dropped. And three windows are still open in state at the end, the last few hours, waiting for later data to close them. The delay is a trade. A longer one keeps more late events and holds more state; a shorter one forgets sooner and drops more. Choose it from how late your data really arrives, which the bronze tables can tell you.

The tracker sends some events twice. In the silver course, drop duplicates on event id took care of that, over a finished table. On a stream it is harder: to know an id is a repeat, Spark must remember every id it has seen, and a stream never ends. Drop duplicates within watermark bounds that memory. With a one hour watermark, an id is remembered until the watermark passes its event time plus an hour, and then forgotten. Three days of clicks go through: three thousand and thirty four read from Kafka. Thirteen copies are dropped, because their first copy was still in state. Eight more events arrived later than the watermark allowed and were dropped for that reason. Three thousand and thirteen events are kept, each id exactly once. At the end, the state holds just sixty five ids, the most recent hour or so, however long the stream runs. The rule to remember: a copy is only caught if it arrives within the window, so the watermark should be longer than the gap between copies, which for a retrying tracker is seconds.

A live count of clicks is more useful by category, and the category is in gold, not in the click. With products joins the stream to the product dimension: it explodes each event's items into one row per product, then joins them to the dim product Delta table on product id. That is a stream static join. The stream side is the micro batches from Kafka. The static side is an ordinary table, read again for every batch, so a product added or renamed in gold appears in the stream's output from the next batch on, with no restart. It needs no state for the static side, because nothing about the table has to be remembered between batches. Counted by category and event type, after two batches, beauty has the most product views, a hundred and twenty six, and the most purchases. One thing streams cannot do is pivot: it would be two aggregations in a row, which Spark refuses on a stream, so the script counts by category and type, and pivots the finished table afterwards. Joining two streams to each other is a different, harder thing: both sides must be held in state until a match can no longer arrive, which again needs watermarks.

The last streaming feature: an alert when someone fills a cart and leaves. A visit has no fixed length, so a tumbling window will not do. A session window is defined by activity instead. The first event opens a window for that visitor, every event within thirty minutes stretches it, and thirty minutes of silence closes it. Abandoned carts groups the stream by visitor and session window, records whether the visit added to the cart and whether it bought, and keeps the visits that carted but never bought. The visitor is the logged in user, or the anonymous id, cast to the same type; the first run failed on exactly that, when the bot's anonymous id met a numeric user id. With a ten minute watermark, a visit is only final once the watermark passes its end, because until then a purchase could still arrive. One day of clicks gives sixty one alerts, each written once. Four visits were still open when the stream stopped: no one can know yet whether they will buy. That is the honest answer a streaming system gives, and why a real alert waits for the watermark rather than firing early.

The last thing the business asks for is the most familiar: recommended for you. Shopwave's customers rate what they buy, from one to five stars, and the reviews now land in the raw data. A new schema reads them, and a new module, ml dot py, starts with a single function that loads them. Nine thousand four hundred and forty seven ratings, from one thousand eight hundred and thirty three customers, on fifty products. As a matrix, customers down the side and products across the top, that is ninety one thousand cells, and fewer than eight percent are filled. The empty cells are not zeros: nobody has said anything about them yet. Recommending means filling them in: guessing what each customer would rate the products they have never tried. Is there anything to learn? The customer with the most ratings, customer one, rates fashion four point six stars on average and books two point two, a full two stars apart. Most customers have a favourite category and one they dislike, and that pattern, hidden in a sparse matrix, is what the model has to find.

Spark's machine learning library is built from two kinds of piece. A transformer turns one DataFrame into another. An estimator learns from a DataFrame and produces a transformer, a model. A pipeline chains them, so that fitting the pipeline fits every stage in order, and the result is one model that can be saved, loaded and applied as a unit. Shopwave's pipeline has two stages. A SQL transformer selects the three columns the algorithm wants: customer, product, and the rating as a float. Then ALS, alternating least squares, the classic collaborative filtering algorithm. Its main settings: rank, how many numbers describe each customer and each product, here eight; a regularization parameter that keeps those numbers small; a fixed seed, because the factors start random; and a cold start strategy of drop, so the model makes no guess for a customer it has never seen. Fitted on every rating, it learns one thousand eight hundred and thirty three customer vectors and fifty product vectors, and transform adds a prediction column. On ratings it has already seen, the guesses are close, which proves nothing yet.

How does ALS fill in the matrix, and why does it suit Spark? It looks for two small matrices whose product approximates the big one: a row of eight numbers for every customer, and a row of eight numbers for every product. A predicted rating is the dot product of a customer's row and a product's row. Finding both at once is hard. But if the products' numbers are fixed, each customer's row is a small least squares problem that can be solved on its own, and the same is true the other way round. So ALS alternates: fix the products, solve every customer; fix the customers, solve every product; ten rounds. Each half is embarrassingly parallel. Spark splits the customers into blocks and the products into blocks, four of each here, and between half steps shuffles each block's factors to where they are needed. The lab's run took five jobs and fifty four stages. The proof is at the bottom: for customer one and product one, the first four of eight numbers on each side, and their dot product, three point eight nine, is exactly the prediction the model gives.

A model has to be judged on ratings it has not seen, and the way it will be used decides how to split them. The model will predict the future from the past, so the split is by time: train on the six thousand two hundred and sixty four ratings before October, test on the three thousand one hundred and eighty three after. The measure is RMSE, roughly how many stars off a guess is. Every model needs a baseline to beat. Giving everyone the average rating is off by one point oh nine stars; giving each product its own average, one point oh. And ALS alone? One point two four: worse than the baselines. That is a real result, and a common one. ALS has no idea that some products are simply better than others, and its regularization pulls every guess toward zero stars. The fix is to let each one do what it is good at: the product's average carries how good a product is, and ALS learns only what the average misses, each customer's taste. The average plus ALS scores zero point nine one, the best of all. Split at random instead, the same model looks slightly better again, because it has trained on December to predict October. That number would be a promise the model could not keep.

A model is only useful once its answers are where the website can read them. The recommend job fits the average plus ALS on every rating so far, then scores every customer against every product: one thousand eight hundred and thirty three customers times fifty products. A window ranks each customer's scores, keeps the best five, and the result is written to a gold Delta table, nine thousand one hundred and sixty five rows, one per customer and rank. Does it make sense? Customer one, from the first section of this course, rates fashion and electronics highest. The five recommendations are sunglasses, a power bank, headphones, a rain jacket and a keyboard: every one of them fashion or electronics. Nobody told the model about categories; it found the taste in the ratings alone. A production version would also leave out what the customer already owns, and refit on a schedule. Course eleven makes this job part of the nightly run.

An honest end to this course: none of it needed Spark. Nine and a half thousand ratings are about one megabyte in memory. This lab answers the same question with pandas and scikit-learn, in one Python process, with no Java and no cluster. It reads the review files, joins each to its product's category, and fits a plain ridge regression on one-hot features: one per customer and category pair, which is exactly a customer's taste, and one per product, its quality. On the same test months, its error is zero point eight eight stars, slightly better than ALS, because those features say directly what ALS had to discover. It reads, fits and scores in well under a second. The point is not that ALS is bad. It is that Spark earns its overhead when the data does not fit on one machine, or keeps arriving, or is already in the lake next to everything else. Shopwave at scale factor one would have two hundred thousand customers and five thousand products, and the year's clicks as implicit feedback would run to tens of millions of rows. That is where Spark's ALS belongs. For a megabyte, use the simplest tool that works: pandas, Polars or DuckDB.

The platform works, but running it means remembering six commands in the right order. Production starts by giving it one front door. Jobs dot py lists every job of the night, in order, each with a line saying what it does and the function that runs it: bronze, silver, gold, the incremental orders load, the change feed merge, and the recommendations. With no arguments, it prints that list, which is now the platform's own documentation. Run with job names, it runs those in the order given; nightly runs them all. They all run in one process, so the night starts one JVM and one Spark session and every job shares it, instead of paying a JVM's start-up for each. And a typo is no longer silent: asking for a job that does not exist prints the usage and the real job names, and exits with an error a scheduler will notice.

Every transform in Shopwave is a function from DataFrames to a DataFrame, which makes it testable without any real data. A test builds a few rows by hand, the cases that matter, calls the transform exactly as the job does, and compares the result to the frame it must give with assert DataFrame equal, from PySpark's own testing module. It compares rows and types, in any order. Three tests here. An order placed at half past eleven at night UTC is already the next day in Berlin, but not in New York. Revenue is quantity times unit price, and an order line whose order does not exist is not a sale. And latest keeps each order's newest change. Pytest is added to requirements. Conftest dot py starts one Spark session for the whole run, with a single shuffle partition and no web UI, because starting a JVM takes seconds and a test on four rows takes milliseconds. Three passed. Tests like these run on every change, before anything reaches the nightly run.

Tests check the code. Checks check the data, every night, after it is built. Checks dot py writes down what gold must be true of. Some are conditions every row must meet: revenue is never negative, quantity is between one and ten, payments are positive in euros, every product has a category. Others are queries that must come back empty: paid orders with no payment, sales of products that do not exist. Each has a level. An error stops the night; a warning is reported and the night goes on. Run against gold, everything passes except one warning: a hundred and ninety one paid orders have no payment. That is the generator's planted problem from the start of the course, a known issue that finance chases, so it is a warning, and the exit code is zero. With strict mode on, the same warning becomes an error, the checks print that the night stops here, and the exit code is one. Checks becomes a job in the nightly run, right after gold, so nothing built on bad data runs after it.

Everything so far ran in local mode: driver and executors in one process. Now the same code runs on a cluster: a standalone Spark master and two workers, started by cluster dot sh. pip's PySpark has no start master script, but it ships the script those call, spark daemon, so the cluster needs nothing beyond the venv. Each worker offers two cores and a gigabyte. The job is submitted with spark submit and a properties file. Two things change once executors are other processes. Python code must travel to them, so the package is zipped and listed as a py file. And whatever the driver's JVM needs from its first moment, the log configuration and Delta's jars, goes in the properties file, because spark submit starts that JVM before session dot py runs; the first run failed to find Delta for exactly that reason, and session dot py now leaves the master to spark submit. The run reports the master's address, two executors and four cores, and how many of revenue by country's tasks each executor ran: both took part, unevenly, and the split changes from run to run, because a task goes to whichever executor has a free core. On real machines, one more thing changes: the data must sit on storage every machine can reach.

Jobs fail and get retried, and history needs rebuilding when a bug is fixed. Both are only safe if running a job twice gives the same result as running it once. Daily dot py builds one day of a daily sales table from gold, and writes it with overwrite and replace where, limited to that day: one Delta commit removes that day's rows and adds the new ones, and every other day is untouched. Built for October the fifth, the table has eleven rows. Built again, still eleven, with the same revenue. A backfill is the same job over a range: the first week of October gives eighty three rows over seven days, and running the whole backfill again gives exactly the same table. Had the job appended instead, every retry would have doubled a day. The rule for production jobs: each one replaces exactly the slice of data it owns.

And here is the whole platform, in one command. Nightly runs every job in order, in one Spark session, starting from nothing but the raw exports. Each job's own output goes to a log file, and the terminal gets one line per job. Bronze lands every source. Silver cleans, conforms and passes its quality gates. Gold builds the star schema as Delta tables, and the checks pass. The orders job loads every order since the high water mark, the change feed is merged into their statuses, and the recommendations are refitted and written. Seven jobs, seven ticks, and the gold folder holds every table the business, the website and the stream read from. If any job fails, the night stops at it, because everything after it would build on what it failed to write. That is the platform this course set out to build, from the first DataFrame to here.

That is the whole platform, built and run, from a first DataFrame to a cluster. To finish, here is what each part becomes at a company's scale, because almost none of the code changes. The compute moves from local mode to a managed platform: Databricks, Amazon EMR, Google Dataproc, or Spark on Kubernetes, where executors are pods. The lake moves from a local folder to object storage: S three, Azure Data Lake or Google Cloud Storage. Delta tables addressed by path get names in a catalog, such as Unity Catalog or AWS Glue, so that people and tools find them by name and permissions live in one place. Apache Iceberg is the other open table format worth knowing; it solves the same problems Delta does. The nightly command becomes a graph of tasks in a scheduler like Airflow or Dagster, with retries and alerts. The single Kafka broker becomes a managed service. Spark Connect separates a thin client from a remote Spark server, which is how notebooks and applications talk to shared clusters now. And the tests and checks run in continuous integration on every change, before anything reaches the nightly run. The ideas you learned stay the same everywhere: partitions and tasks, shuffles, plans, memory, and tables with a transaction log.
